notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense puts the snakes' approach before the reader's eyes, as if Aeneas were watching it happen again as he speaks.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Placing the verb early stresses the winding movement of the snakes before we see their huge backs.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: A second present tense keeps the scene vivid: the coils seem to be moving now.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: Adjective and noun are split across the line, so the huge backs seem to stretch out over the whole line, just as the snakes stretch over the sea.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The short present-tense verb opening the line makes the noise sudden and immediate.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.trans: the sound of the foaming sea
notes.body: The repeated s sounds imitate the hiss of the foam, and of the snakes themselves.

notes.label: Variatio
notes.trans: deep, open sea, waves, sea, salt sea
notes.body: Virgil uses five different words for the sea in a few lines, which keeps the description fresh and makes the sea seem vast and ever-present.

notes.label: Pairing
notes.body: Blood and fire are paired to describe the snakes' eyes, which makes them seem both murderous and unnatural.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The phrase is held to the end of the line, so the reader is left with the terrifying image of eyes burning red.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The verb comes early, so the reader sees the snakes' flickering tongues before anything else.

notes.label: Alliteration and sibilance
notes.trans: licking their hissing mouths with flickering tongues
notes.body: The repeated l and s sounds imitate the hissing and flicking of the snakes' tongues.

notes.label: Framing word order
notes.body: sibila opens the line and ora closes it, so the hissing mouths surround the tongues, just as they do in reality.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The first word shows the Trojans' panic at once: they run in all directions before we are told why.

notes.label: Military language
notes.body: agmen is the word for an army on the march, so the snakes advance like soldiers. This may hint at the Greek army that will soon pour into Troy.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: Laocoön's name opens the line, so the reader knows at once who the snakes are hunting.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense makes the attack immediate and unstoppable.

notes.label: Interwoven word order
notes.trans: the small bodies of his two sons
notes.body: The adjectives and nouns are interlaced (parva duorum corpora natorum), just as the snake winds itself around the boys.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense brings the reader right into the horror as the snake wraps round the boys.

notes.label: Enjambment
notes.body: The verb is carried over to the start of a new line, so the reader has to wait for the moment the snake strikes.

notes.label: Pathos
notes.body: Virgil calls the boys' limbs "wretched", which shows the narrator's pity and invites the reader to share it.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The repeated m sound links the pitiful limbs with the bite that devours them.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: depascitur is used of animals grazing, so the snakes seem to feed on the boys like cattle on grass. The present tense makes it horribly immediate.

notes.label: Framing word order
notes.body: miseros and artus frame the end of the line, so the boys' pitiful limbs surround the snakes' feeding.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The verb opens the line and its sentence, so the sudden attack on Laocoön himself hits the reader with force.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense makes the attack feel as if it is happening now.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: Another present tense keeps the pace fast as the snakes tie Laocoön up.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: spiris and ingentibus are separated by the verb, so the coils seem to wrap around the action itself.

notes.label: Anaphora
notes.trans: twice round his waist, twice round his neck
notes.body: Repeating bis at the start of each phrase stresses how completely the snakes wrap him, coil after coil.

notes.label: Alliteration
notes.body: The hard c sounds and the s of squamea give the line a harsh, hissing sound as the coils tighten.

notes.label: Hyperbaton
notes.body: The adjective ends line 218 and the noun begins line 219, so the snakes' scaly backs stretch over the line break just as they stretch around Laocoön.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The verb comes early, stressing the snakes' dominance as they rise above their victim.

notes.label: Historic present
notes.body: The present tense leaves the reader with a vivid picture of the snakes towering over Laocoön.

notes.label: Tmesis
notes.body: circum and dati belong together as one verb, circumdati ("wound around"), but Virgil splits them across the line. The coils of the word wrap round squamea terga just as the snakes wrap round Laocoön.

notes.label: Laocoön
notes.body: A Trojan priest of Neptune who had warned the Trojans not to trust the horse and had hurled his spear into its side (lines 40–53). He was sacrificing a bull to Neptune on the shore when the snakes came.

questions: How does Virgil make the snakes seem both animal and almost like an army in lines 208–213?
Why do you think the snakes attack the two boys before their father? What is the effect on the reader?
Choose three sound effects in this section and explain how each one helps you picture the scene.

context.body:
The death of Laocoön and his sons is also shown in one of the most famous sculptures of the ancient world, a marble group found in Rome in 1506 and now in the Vatican Museums. The writer Pliny the Elder saw it in the palace of the emperor Titus and names three sculptors from Rhodes: Hagesander, Polydorus and Athenodorus.

Scholars still argue whether the statue inspired Virgil, Virgil inspired the statue, or both go back to an earlier Greek source. If you can, look at a picture of it and compare how the sculptor and the poet each show the father's struggle and the sons' suffering.
